passage: In Vienna, Vera had put up with Selin's taunts about her accent for six weeks: every corridor, every group photo. One evening she made a plan in her bedroom: an edited picture of Selin, a mocking caption, and a post on the class channel at midnight so everyone would see. "She deserves it," Vera told her friend Lena, who wrote back, "Are you sure?" Vera posted it anyway. By morning Selin had posted something crueler, and the class split into two camps. At break the head teacher called both girls to the office. The first question was about the post. The taunts, which Vera had never reported, were not mentioned at all, and both girls lost a week on the school channel.

qa.q: How long had Vera put up with Selin's taunts?
qa.a: Vera had put up with them for six weeks.

qa.q: What was Vera feeling when she made the plan in her bedroom?
qa.a: Vera felt angry and humiliated, and wanted Selin to feel the same way.

qa.q: What could Vera do instead, and why?
qa.a: Vera could show the taunts to a teacher or counsellor and keep a record, because that puts the original harm at the centre and does not risk punishment.

qa.q: How might Selin see Vera's post?
qa.a: Selin would probably see it as an attack and feel embarrassed and defensive, which fits with answering it with something crueler.

grounding: Angry at repeated taunts, the student plans to embarrass the bully online, which escalates, leads to punishment for both, and shifts attention from the original harm.

subtype: Approach: silent endurance hoping it stops [Pitfall]
passage:
Madhuri: hey. you've missed school 3 days this week
Ritu: just tired
Madhuri: last week too. and you stopped coming to lunch
Ritu: I'm fine
Madhuri: I don't think you are. is it the back row group?
Ritu: it's been going on since July. I thought if I ignored it, it would stop
Madhuri: and it hasn't?
Ritu: no. now I keep thinking about not going in at all. it feels like the only way to get a break
Madhuri: that sounds really heavy. I'm glad you told me. it isn't your fault
Madhuri: tell your mum tonight. tomorrow I'll come with you to see the counsellor and stay next to you
Ritu: ok. mum tonight. I'll try

qa.q: Since when had it been going on, according to Ritu?
qa.a: It had been going on since July.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when saying 'I thought if I ignored it, it would stop'?
qa.a: Ritu felt hopeful at first and is now worn down and stuck, since ignoring it has not worked and staying away seems like the only relief.

qa.q: What could Ritu and Madhuri do to make sure it is handled safely, and why?
qa.a: Ritu could tell the mum that night and see the counsellor the next day with Madhuri, because adults can act on it and Ritu no longer carries it alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri to hear this?
qa.a: Madhuri is probably worried and caring, noticing the missed days and the missed lunches, and glad Ritu opened up. 🤍

grounding: The student ignores the bullying and says nothing for months, and it continues, self-confidence drops, and avoiding school starts to seem like the only relief.

subtype: Approach: bystander friend choosing to support [Action]
passage: The canteen was packed and the bell was five minutes away when Sumit noticed Ishita sitting alone, a boy from 10B leaning over her tray, whispering something that made two others laugh. Ishita stared at her rice. Sumit's heart thumped, but he did not laugh. He put his tray down beside Ishita and sat. "Stop it," he said evenly, loud enough for the boy to hear. "That isn't funny." The boy shrugged and left, and the laughing died. Ishita let out a breath. "Thanks. I didn't know what to do." After lunch Sumit went to the class teacher, told the teacher what he had seen and offered to say it again if needed. "You did the right thing," the teacher said. That evening Ishita texted: "Can we sit together tomorrow too?"

qa.q: Where did Sumit see Ishita being teased?
qa.a: In the canteen, where the boy from 10B was leaning over Ishita's tray.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when he sat beside Ishita?
qa.a: Sumit was nervous, shown by his thumping heart, but chose to support Ishita anyway.

qa.q: What else could Sumit do if the boy came back, and why?
qa.a: Sumit could ask other friends to sit with Ishita and report again to the teacher, because more visible support makes it harder to continue and adults can step in.

qa.q: How does Ishita see Sumit's choice to sit down?
qa.a: Ishita feels relieved and less alone, since Sumit sat beside her and spoke up, which is why Ishita asks to sit together again.

grounding: A friend who witnesses it sits beside the target, does not laugh, tells the bully to stop when it feels safe, and reports it to a teacher afterwards, showing that visible support matters.

subtype: Approach: bystander staying quiet out of fear [Pitfall]
passage: At the back of a classroom in Madrid, Dalia watched three girls copy Ines's way of speaking and giggle whenever Ines answered a question. It had been going on for weeks. Dalia opened her mouth once and closed it again. What if they started on her? She had seen what happened to the last person who spoke up. So she looked down at her worksheet. At break Ines ate alone by the wall, and Dalia, two benches away, chewed slowly and said nothing. The mocking got louder on Thursday. On Friday Ines did not come to class. Dalia told herself it was not her fault and that she could not have changed anything, and she hated how well that sounded.

qa.q: Who did Dalia see being mocked?
qa.a: Dalia saw Ines being mocked by three girls.

qa.q: What is Dalia afraid of, and how does it show?
qa.a: Dalia is afraid of becoming the next target, shown by opening and closing her mouth and looking down at her worksheet.

qa.q: What could Dalia do next, and why?
qa.a: Dalia could sit with Ines at break and tell a teacher what she has seen, because company and an adult report are lower-risk ways to help.

qa.q: How might Ines see Dalia's silence?
qa.a: Ines likely feels isolated, eating alone by the wall while a classmate who sees everything says nothing.

grounding: A classmate sees the teasing but fears becoming the next target and stays silent, which is understandable but leaves the victim isolated and the behaviour unchecked.

passage: I ride the same bus as Sarika, so I noticed. Last Monday Sarika came out of the counsellor's room with a folded sheet. On it was a rough map: the back seats of the bus, the corridor by the science lab, the stairs near the gym, each marked with a red dot. By Wednesday Sarika was sitting in the front seats near the driver and the bus attendant, and walking the corridor with two friends. Someone had also given Sarika a small card with three names to go to quickly: the counsellor, the class teacher and the PT sir. On Thursday I saw Sarika glance back at the corridor and then keep walking. I don't know how Sarika feels. But Sarika didn't look as tense as last week. - Mridul

qa.q: What places were marked on the map Sarika carried?
qa.a: The back seats of the bus, the corridor by the science lab and the stairs near the gym.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling, and how sure can Mridul be?
qa.a: Sarika may feel a bit safer, since Sarika looked less tense, though Mridul says plainly not knowing how Sarika feels.

qa.q: What else could Sarika and the counsellor add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: They could set a time to review how it is working, because places and people change and the plan should change with them.

qa.q: How might the two friends who walk with Sarika experience this?
qa.a: They probably feel useful and protective, glad to be trusted with a clear job.

grounding: The student, with a counsellor, identifies where the bullying occurs, such as the bus or corridor, and arranges to walk with friends, sit near the staff and know whom to approach quickly.

subtype: Approach: blocking and reporting online abuse [Action]
passage:
Sudha: Show me the phone. Salma, breathe. Which accounts?
Salma: These three. They keep posting my photo with names.
Sudha: Okay. First, your settings. Make your profile private. Yes, here.
Salma: Done.
Sudha: Now block each one. Don't reply. Not a word.
Salma: Blocked. Should I delete the posts?
Sudha: No. Screenshot them first, with the date showing. We keep those.
Salma: Okay. Saved.
Sudha: There's a report button under each post. Choose harassment. Do it for all three.
Salma: Reported. It feels a bit better.
Sudha: Tonight we show Mummy. Tomorrow we give the screenshots to your class teacher. You are not doing this alone.
Salma: Thank you, didi.

qa.q: What did Sudha tell Salma to do before deleting anything?
qa.a: Sudha told Salma to screenshot the posts with the date showing.

qa.q: How does Salma feel after reporting the posts?
qa.a: Salma feels a bit better and less exposed, though still shaken, as the steps give some control.

qa.q: What else could Salma and Sudha do if new accounts appear, and why?
qa.a: They could block and report each new account and add the screenshots to the record, because the school can then see the whole pattern.

qa.q: How does Sudha see the situation?
qa.a: Sudha is calm and protective, guiding Salma step by step and insisting that adults be told, so Salma is not alone.

grounding: The student uses privacy settings, blocks the accounts, reports the abusive posts on the platform and keeps screenshots for the school, limiting exposure while preserving evidence.

subtype: Approach: following up when the first step fails [Revision]
passage:
Dear Lalit,

You asked how things are at school, so here it is. I told my class teacher about the name-calling on the 4th. The teacher said, "I'll have a word." Nothing changed, and it got worse in the corridor. I have been writing every incident in a notebook: date, time, place, who saw. My parents read it and wrote a letter to the principal with copies of my pages attached. Three days later the principal called us in with the class teacher and the counsellor. There is a plan now: the boys' seats have been moved, a teacher stands in the corridor at break, and we review on the 20th. It isn't over, but things are moving because we kept pushing calmly. I'll write again after the 20th.

Ganga

qa.q: What did Ganga write in the notebook for every incident?
qa.a: Ganga wrote the date, time, place and who saw.

qa.q: How does Ganga feel about the situation now?
qa.a: Ganga feels cautiously hopeful, saying it isn't over but things are moving because they kept pushing calmly.

qa.q: What could Ganga do if the plan does not work by the 20th, and why?
qa.a: Ganga could go back to the principal with the updated notebook and ask about the next step in the policy, because official channels can escalate when needed.

qa.q: How might Ganga's parents feel about writing to the principal?
qa.a: The parents are probably worried and determined, wanting Ganga protected and willing to press until action is taken.

grounding: When a single teacher conversation changes nothing, the parents write to the principal and the student keeps recording incidents, escalating calmly through official channels until action is taken.

passage: For months after the bullying at his school in Hanoi, Bao went straight home each day. With the school counsellor he began weekly talks. On Wednesdays the counsellor helped him name what had happened and reminded him none of it was his fault. He joined a climbing club, where Lucia, a girl from the year above, taught him to belay, and where being scared and doing it anyway felt normal. By spring he had three friends he ate lunch with. A year later the counsellor asked if Bao would talk to the Year 7s. Bao stood in front of them for ten minutes. "If someone keeps making you feel small, tell one adult early," he said. "Don't wait like I did." A boy at the back nodded.

qa.q: Who taught Bao to belay at the climbing club?
qa.a: Lucia, a girl from the year above, taught Bao to belay.

qa.q: How did Bao feel at the climbing club, and what does it show?
qa.a: Bao felt more capable and less alone there, since being scared and doing it anyway began to feel normal.

qa.q: What else could Bao do to keep helping younger students, and why?
qa.a: Bao could offer to be a lunchtime buddy for Year 7s who feel left out, because early company and a trusted person make speaking up easier.

qa.q: How might the boy at the back of the room have felt?
qa.a: The boy probably felt understood and encouraged, since someone older spoke openly about waiting too long.

grounding: With help from a counsellor, sport and a small circle of supportive friends, the student regains confidence, and later helps younger students recognise bullying and speak up early.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of late nights [Thinking]
passage: Thabo's phone said 3:07 again. In Johannesburg the house was silent and he was awake, scrolling. At lunch that day, Yara had asked how he got through the week on so little sleep, and Thabo realised he had never asked himself why. That night he drew three columns: when I really go to bed, what I do from six to ten, what I do after. The answers were plain. From six to ten he watched videos and called it resting. He started studying at ten, when guilt kicked in. After a stressful day he scrolled to switch his head off, until three. The day had enough hours; he was spending the best ones on avoiding. At the bottom of the page he wrote: "Study six to eight. Phone off the bed."

qa.q: What time did Thabo's phone show?
qa.a: The phone said 3:07.

qa.q: What did Thabo realise about the late nights?
qa.a: Thabo realised that he was spending the early evening on videos and starting to study late out of guilt, then scrolling after a stressful day.

qa.q: What other step could Thabo try, and why?
qa.a: Thabo could do a short walk or talk to Yara after a stressful day instead of scrolling, because it lets the head wind down without eating into the night.

qa.q: How might Yara see Thabo's tiredness?
qa.a: Yara probably worries and wonders how Thabo copes, having asked at lunch how he gets through the week on so little sleep.

grounding: A student sleeping at 3 am asks why, and finds it comes from late-night scrolling after a stressful day and studying during the evening's wasted hours, not from a lack of hours in the day.

passage: Damini had been going to bed at three for months, and the maths exam was three weeks away. Jumping to ten at night would only mean lying awake, so she chose small steps. Asif, her classmate, agreed to phone at seven every morning so her wake-up time stayed fixed. Bedtime went to quarter to three for three days, then half past two, then quarter past, then two. On the ninth night a wedding band began playing drums in the next lane and she almost gave up the plan. She kept the wake-up time anyway, was tired the next day, and held the step. Twelve days later she was asleep by two and waking without the call. It was not ten yet, but it was moving.

qa.q: What time did Asif phone Damini each morning?
qa.a: Asif phoned at seven every morning.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling on the ninth night, and what did she do?
qa.a: Damini felt tempted to give up because of the wedding drums, but she kept the wake-up time and held the step.

qa.q: What else could Damini do to keep moving towards an earlier bedtime, and why?
qa.a: Damini could keep a lamp-off routine and dim screens before each new step, because a steady wind-down makes the earlier time easier to keep.

qa.q: How might Asif see the morning calls?
qa.a: Asif probably sees them as a small way to help a classmate before the exam and is pleased when the calls are no longer needed.

grounding: Instead of jumping from 3 am to 10 pm, the student moves bedtime earlier by fifteen minutes every few days, keeping a fixed wake-up time so the body clock adjusts steadily.
